The terms of the Agreement are generally balanced and, as the contract value is £0 at this stage, we consider the Agreement to be low risk.

That being said, please see below some key points that we have flagged for your attention:

* *Scope of services (pg 2):* CBRE will act as Bolt’s “+sole agents”+, i.e. this is an +exclusive agreement+ with CBRE. We assume this reflects the agreed position, however if you will be using other agents for the same/similar services, +the wording will need to be amended+.
* *Scope of services (pg 2):* please check that the list of services set out on page 2 to be provided by CBRE are correct and sufficiently cover Bolt’s requirements.
* *Acquisition fee (pg 3):* note that on completion of an acquisition, a “finder’s fee” (the sum of which at this stage is unknown) may be agreed between CBRE and Bolt and is to be payable by Bolt.
* *clauses 2.2 and 2.3 (pg 6):* note that Bolt will need to pay any out-of-pocket expenses such as marketing material, travelling costs, photocopying, printing etc, though CBRE will obtain estimates for the costs of marketing materials and such costs will be agreed with Bolt before being incurred. For completeness and clarity, clause 2.3 would ideally state that +any+ out-of-pocket expenses and costs (not just in relation to marketing materials) will be agreed with Bolt prior to being incurred.
* *clause 2.6 (pg 6):* note that CBRE has the right to revise their fees after the first 6 months of the Agreement, and on a 6 monthly basis thereafter. Bolt will be notified of any change and must provide its consent to such change, but flagging for your information.
* *clause 3.1 (pg 6):* invoices must be paid within 30 days of issue. This is standard drafting, but flagging for your information.
* *clause 5.4 (pg 7):* CBRE’s liability is capped at 25% of the property value or £20 million (whichever is +lower+). However, Bolt’s liability is *uncapped*, meaning there's no limit to what CBRE could potentially claim in return. Although the likelihood of this risk materialising is low at this stage (as we are not currently paying any fees and we are the customer under this arrangement), we are flagging this point for your information. Where possible, we seek to cap (i.e. limit) our liability, however on the basis that this Agreement is low value and there is limited scope to negotiate CBRE’s standard terms, we are comfortable with the risk here.
* *clause 7.1.2 (pg 8):* note that both parties have the right to terminate for convenience - this means that Bolt has the right to terminate for any reason by giving 3 months’ written notice. As the Agreement does not specify the length of the Agreement, it is likely to be considered a “rolling” contract, meaning that it will continue indefinitely until terminated. Consider whether 3 months’ notice is acceptable in practice.
* *clause 7.1.3 (pg 8):* note also that CBRE has the right to terminate the Agreement if it “reasonably anticipates” that Bolt will not pay an invoice on time. This is low risk as (a) we are currently not paying any fees under this Agreement and (b) we understand that invoices are typically paid on time, but flagging for your attention.
* *Data Processing Annex (pg 10 - 12):* we understand from the details provided in your ticket that no personal data is processed. If you are comfortable with all of the above-mentioned points, we are happy for the Agreement to be signed.

To clarify based on the legal structure under POPIA:

* 🔒 The move towards "hard opt-in" relates specifically to Section 69(2) — i.e., when approaching non-customers for consent under Section 69(1)(a). The Regulator's emphasis on written consent and use of Form 4 applies *only when no existing customer relationship exists* and hard consent is required.

!Screenshot 2025-04-30 at 17.13.26.png|width=874,height=624,alt="Screenshot 2025-04-30 at 17.13.26.png"!

* ✅ Section 69(1)(b) explicitly permits direct marketing via electronic communication where the data subject _is a customer_ of the responsible party, _subject to subsection (3)_.
* ✅ Section 69(3) outlines the conditions under which this "soft opt-in" approach is valid — essentially matching what you've described:
** Existing customer relationship
** Marketing of similar products/services
** Clear opportunity to opt out at collection and in every message

So yes — we're aligned: *soft opt-in is still permissible under POPIA* when all the conditions of 69(3) are met.

+*BACKGROUND*+

* Bolt intends to enter a partnership with a Croatian bank (ZABA)to run a discount-based campaign in the Bolt app.
** Campaign will work as follows:
*** Bolt users with eligible ZABA cards (filtered by BINs) will receive a discount on Bolt rides. 
*** ZABA will cover the cost of this discount.
** Concept is similar to existing BIN-based promotions in Ukraine and Azerbaijan (with Visa).
** Campaign will be targeted, with specified duration, location (Croatia) and specific target users (users who have ZABA cards).
** Pop messages / banner / newsletter will be circulated with info about partnership/discount (to attract more users to use bank card and to attract more users for bank)
* No user data will be shared with ZABA.
* Questions:
** Can we share details about the promotion via newsletter to all users in Croatia, regardless of whether they are eligible?
** Can we send push notifications about the promotion to all users in Croatia?
** Can we place a banner in the app that’s visible to all Croatian users, even if the discount applies only to ZABA cardholders?
** In case we cannot do any of things mentioned above, what can be done, and how can we execute partnership?

+*ANALYSIS*+

* Data sharing:
** Provided that no personal data is being shared, this raises no privacy issues. Data sharing agreement will not be needed.
** However, worth checking for good measure, as I am surprised to hear that no data sharing will be needed.
* Marketing comms:
** Can we send them to all users in Croatia?
*** The product/service that we are promoting here belongs to a third party (ZABA). As such, we will need to rely on user consent (as promoting ZABA cards is not promoting a similar product/service to those already provided by Bolt), rather than the soft opt-in, if this counts as _direct_ marketing. 
**** This in turn would suggest that we would not be able to send the comms to all users - only those that have consented.
*** As such, the key question is whether these forms of marketing are _direct._
**** Direct marketing = Marketing directed at _particular individuals_. Personally addressed to email, or online ad that is targeted based on activity (e.g., browsing history, login information etc.).
**** All three mediums should be ok in this context - none of them are direct. They are all indiscriminate / mass marketing. However, banner is better than newsletter (if sent by email) and push notifications.
*** This suggests {color:#36b37e}*we do not need to rely on consent here, as this is not caught as ‘direct marketing’.* {color}Instead, we can rely on legitimate interests when processing a user’s country information to send them these mass marketing comms.
**** However, the banner would be better than the newsletter and the push notifications, as the latter could technically be considered direct in a sense. For those, we would need to ensure that the user has opted into ‘partner offers’.
** Any other requirements?
*** We can use a user’s country to send them marketing materials. This will be covered in the updated driver privacy notice, which will be launched soon.
*** For good measure, we should ensure that the users can opt out of the push notifications / newsletter (if sent via email), just in case it is classified as direct marketing. Presumably this would be available via the app settings anyway.

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* Questions:
** It is mentioned that we will not be sharing any user data with ZABA. If so, how will ZABA know how much fo the bill to foot? Aggregated stats or a lump sum ,for example?
** How will we know if users have ZABA cards (will we be reviewing their payment method on their account)?
** Request copies of the Visa agreements.
** How will the newsletter be circulated? Via email, or just available in the Bolt app?
* Advice:
** Banners - Yes, we can send this to all users in Croatia.
** Push notifications / newsletters - This is trickier. Would be better to ensure that the user has consented to this (which poses a risk to mass marketing

Q: if it’s easier/better to always add new members to the policy itself OR if we are keeping a shared cluster if we can just share the cluster indeed and not worry about new member

A: Always add new member will make sure the pipeline development is more secured. Especially if the group has access to data that the other policy doesn’t have. Except you don’t have any concern if someone use your shared cluster to access your data or adding cost to your cost-center. Example from incentive team: [https://taxify.slack.com/archives/CF65PRL0N/p1746010871065519?thread_ts=1746007789.981239&cid=CF65PRL0N|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/CF65PRL0N/p1746010871065519?thread_ts=1746007789.981239&cid=CF65PRL0N|smart-link]

It can be prevented though with cluster permission that you have already done.

!Screenshot 2025-05-02 at 09.03.13.png|width=481,height=368,alt="Screenshot 2025-05-02 at 09.03.13.png"!


Q: which other benefits does being member to the cluster have? For example, can I read from our s3 bucket if I only have access to the cluster or do I also need to be part of the group?
A:  Being member of the group also can create/use personal cluster and job (special usage with additional libraries) (not only shared all-purpose cluster). The access is used to develop pipeline, not only use/see the data. All purpose cluster should be used for development or exploratory purpose.

AFAIR, having access to the cluster can read from S3 bucket and make the cluster creator owner accountable of the action. If it has dangerous action, it could be tracked from audit log. Do you have tested it to give someone who is not part of the group and have access the cluster?


Q: Are there other limitations that would require being part of the group itself?
A: The previous flow user needs to request from Service Desk with their manager approval. However, Compute Team just released unified authorisation to make the access control easier [https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C042BBYF7DH/p1746007631935209|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C042BBYF7DH/p1746007631935209|smart-link]  here. If you are using unified authorisation, each schema access can be managed by your team instead.

Hi all,

Thanks for looping me in.

Looking at what’s been shared, here’s my view:

+*Do we have Insurance?:*+

Unfortunately, we do not have any business insurance to respond to this loss. 

Specifically:

* We do not have *Non-Owned Motor Liability* in Europe to cover physical damage to rented vehicles.
* Our *Public Liability* and *Third-Party Liability* policies explicitly exclude motor vehicle damage, whether the vehicle is owned or hired.
* We have no separate *rental excess* or *hired vehicle damage* cover in place that could be triggered here.

So, from an insurance perspective, this would be treated as an uninsured internal cost.

+*My Recommendation: Push Back on AVIS:*+

I recommend we challenge the DKK 92,603.97 charge for several reasons:



# *Gross Negligence Is Not Clear-Cut*

Yes, the driver misjudged the height restriction, but the photos show damage limited to the roof panel, consistent with a low-speed impact. There’s no visible structural or internal damage, and no sign of deliberate or reckless behaviour (e.g. ignoring flashing signage, speeding, etc.).

It looks like AVIS is leaning on Danish Law L534 regarding reckless driving, but in this case, that feels like an overreach. While the rental contract cites L534, that legislation is aimed at extreme, high-risk behaviours, such as driving over 200 km/h, excessive speeding, drunk driving (BAC > 2.0), and street racing. This incident doesn’t meet that threshold by any reasonable interpretation.

 For reference, the full legislative text is here (in Danish):
 [https://www.retsinformation.dk/eli/lta/2021/534|https://www.retsinformation.dk/eli/lta/2021/534|smart-link] 

The use of L534 here appears inappropriate and seems intended to justify bypassing the standard excess cap.

# *Cost Appears Inflated*

The amount being claimed is high for what appears to be isolated bodywork damage. We should request a full itemised breakdown, including parts, labour, downtime, and admin charges, and reserve the right to challenge the basis for the cost.

# *Corporate Hire – Not Solomon’s Liability*
This was clearly a corporate rental under Bolt’s name, with “_all employees authorised to drive_.” Solomon happened to use his Revolut for payment, but liability sits with the company. AVIS should not be attempting to recover funds via his personal card.
# *Precedent from Past Incident*
We had a near-identical case just over two years ago with Enterprise in Italy, also involving roof damage from a low bridge; it was initially classed as gross negligence. We challenged the classification, and they ultimately dropped it and (from memory) significantly reduced the cost.

Let me know if you’d like me to assist you with drafting a formal reply to AVIS Denmark, but sadly, from an insurance point of view, we do not have any.

One more important point regarding the reference to Danish Law L534 in the rental agreement:

While AVIS may contractually reference L534 (the Danish reckless driving legislation) as a basis for removing the excess cap, my understanding is only the Danish authorities; such as the police or courts, can formally determine whether reckless driving has occurred under that law.

In this case, there is:

* No police involvement
* No legal citation
* No vehicle impoundment or seizure

So, since there’s no legal finding of reckless driving, nor any indication that this incident meets the strict thresholds defined in L534 (e.g. extreme speeding, DUI, street racing, etc.).

It appears AVIS is internally classifying the incident as gross negligence to bypass the usual insurance protection, so we should be clear that this is a contractual interpretation, not a legal one.

This distinction strengthens our argument for pushing back, particularly given the facts of the case: a low-speed clearance misjudgement, no third-party involvement, and no criminal offence, none of which reasonably meet the legal or common-sense threshold for “reckless driving”.

{quote}I’m wondering - how do we approach this? Does it mean that we should have had a bigger investment to be able to detect impact?{quote}

This is regarding how we set the minimum investment required to observe any impact that makes sense for us unit-economics wise. 
For FR partnership we took the older approach because that gave us the advantage of manually running the pre-analysis notebook to check whether we could launch the experiment (as we wanted to launch as soon as possible). In the older approach, we check how many signups we need to generate and then calculate how much investment is required so that after acquiring the users, *our payback will be within 12 months*. 

In the newer version of the notebook, we use a new approach to calculate the required budget. Here also we check how many signups we need to generate to detect impact and then calculate how much investment is required so that after acquiring the users, *our iROI will be within the threshold*. In the new approach, generally the budget required is  much more than that of the older version. For partnership channels that’s a big blocker to spend such high amount required ie. 3K daily for Paris. 

Good news is that we have now updated the older version of the pre-analysis notebook as well with the new budget calculation. For BCN, we have many more tests lined up in other markets. If they are successful, we can revisit Paris again. For now the conclusion is that we invested 600 daily (the actual budget was around 380, so we invested more anyway), but we haven’t received the minimum number of signups to have a payback of 12 months from the campaign. 

{quote}For other experiments. do we also consider this a sign of incrementality absence or treat as an issue with the experiment itself{quote}

Generally we consider them *inconclusive* if the trend reversal is significant and consider them *absence of incrementality* if we don’t have a significant result (this case).

We have now received advice from External Counsel on the claim raised by Lime. See full advice below: 

+*LIVERPOOL CITY COUNCIL ADVICE*+ 

As you are all aware a claim was raised by Lime Technology Limited (“*Lime*”) under the Concession Contracts Regulations 2016 (the “*Regulations*”) against Liverpool City Council (the “*Council*”), in connection with the conduct of a procurement for the award of a concession agreement. Bolt has been identified as the successful tenderer.

Once legal proceedings begin (i.e. when the claim form is served on the Council), the Council must not enter into the concession agreement with Bolt. *This restriction - known as an “automatic suspension”* - remains in place until:

_a) the Court lifts the suspension through an interim order (a temporary ruling made while the case is ongoing); or_

_b) the legal proceedings are resolved, withdrawn, or otherwise concluded, and no further order keeps the suspension in place (such as during an appeal or the possibility of one)._

{color:#006644}*STRENGTH OF GROUNDS*{color}

The grounds raised in the claim form focus on +two points+:

# {color:#0747a6}*Bolt’s pricing*{color}{color:#0747a6}:{color} it is implied that the score awarded to Bolt’s pricing submission was “_abnormally high_”, indicating that the Council “_failed lawfully to apply the award criteria relating to abnormally high pricing submissions_” and/or breached its duties of transparency and equal treatment; and
# {color:#0747a6}*Bolt’s compliance with the requirements of the specification*{color}{color:#0747a6}:{color} the selection questionnaire required that the winning tenderer must: (i) hold “_Full CoMo Bike Share Accreditation_”; and (ii) “_have experience of operating an  e-scooter and e-bike share service in the United Kingdom_.” Lime claims that the Council didn’t apply these rules to Bolt’s bid - implying that Bolt wouldn’t have met the requirements if they had. 

{color:#0747a6}*BOLT’S PRICING*{color}{color:#0747a6}: {color}Regarding the issue of pricing, we assume the reference to “_abnormally high pricing submissions_” means that Bolt has offered a relatively high price for the opportunity to run the concession. There is no provision in the Regulations dealing with “_abnormally high_” prices. Lime has, however, indicated that the ITT – at paragraphs 7.9 – 7.12 – deals with abnormally high pricing submissions and that the Council failed to apply those criteria.

On review of paragraphs 7.9 – 7.12 of the ITT (per the version held on external counsels file), we cannot see why these have been referenced in an argument about abnormally high pricing. The paragraphs simply deal with the totalling of scores, the consensus meeting and how tied scores are to be dealt with. We note that paragraph 8.1 of the ITT provides that: “_The Tender submission will be assessed against the award criteria set out in this ITT and the award of the contract will be made on the basis of the Tender which is the most economically advantageous, subject to the Authority’s right to reject abnormally low tenders_.” There does not, however, seem to us to be a clear assertion as to what the Council has failed to do, as regards paragraphs 7.9 – 7.12.

Since neither the ITT nor the Concession Regulations set out clear rules for handling unusually high or low bids, we have considered how this would be treated under the Public Contracts Regulations 2015. If this were a standard service contract (rather than a concession), the Council would be required to follow the rules on “abnormally low tenders” in those Regulations. In essence, these rules require the Council to investigate any bid that appears unusually low - although the term “abnormally low” isn’t clearly defined. The Council could only reject such a bid if, after reviewing the bidder’s explanation and any supporting evidence, it concludes that the low price or costs cannot be properly justified. 

If the argument is that the Council should have undertaken a similar verification process for “abnormally high” pricing, it follows that the Council should have asked/may now need to ask for evidence from Bolt that the pricing offered can be satisfactorily accounted for, _if_ they considered the price to be abnormal.

As for the strength of this argument: claims based on abnormally low or high pricing are generally hard to win. That’s because it’s not the price alone that matters - it’s whether the contracting authority followed the proper process to check the price. External Counsels view is  the chances of this argument succeeding in court are{color:#ff5630} {color}{color:#ff5630}+*below 50%*+{color}, especially since there doesn’t seem to be a clear legal obligation for the Council to carry out that price-checking process. And even if they didn’t do it at the time, they could still do it now. However, external counsel believe{color:#ff5630} +*there is a greater chance that the Council might decide to abandon the current process and start over*+{color}{color:#ff5630}.{color} See below for more on this point.

{color:#0747a6}*BOLT’S COMPLIANCE WITH THE SPECIFICATION REQUIREMENTS:*{color} appears to be a stronger ground for Lime’s challenge - provided Lime is factually correct. In general, selection-stage criteria that are assessed on a pass/fail basis are more clear-cut than award-stage criteria, which allow for more evaluator judgment and discretion. If Lime can show that Bolt failed to meet the mandatory selection requirements and should not have progressed further, then the Council would have a narrower basis to defend its decision. While evaluators are usually given broad discretion when scoring tenders, that flexibility doesn’t apply in the same way to strict pass/fail conditions

That said, this argument only holds if Limes allegation is factually accurate. Bolt is, naturally, in a better position than external counsel to assess that. If the facts do support the claim, external counsel believe there is a {color:#ff5630}+*greater than 50% chance that this argument would succeed in court*+{color}{color:#ff5630}.{color}

{color:#0747a6}*Likelihood of the tender being abandoned and re-run:* {color}serving the claim form has triggered the automatic suspension, which prevents the Council from signing the contract with Bolt for now. +*As a result, there is a real possibility that the Council may decide to cancel the current process and start the procurement again.*+ 

{color:#0747a6}*The strength of Limes legal arguments is just one factor in assessing whether the Council might abandon the procurement. Other important considerations include:*{color}

_(i) whether the current contract can be extended (and at what cost) to allow time for a new tender process;_

_(ii) the cost and effort involved in starting over;_

_(iii) any political pressure to move quickly with the new contract;_

_(iv) the Council’s usual approach to defending or settling legal claims; and_

_(v) whether the Council is aware of other potential issues with the current procurement._

It’s common for claimants to rely on the automatic suspension as a way to increase pressure on the authority. While external counsel can't comment on the Council’s internal politics, external counsel's experience suggests that authorities often give serious consideration to cancelling and restarting a process - especially when they can extend the current contract without major additional cost.

{color:#0747a6}+*TACTICAL CONSIDERATIONS FOR BOLT*+{color}

* From a tactical perspective, Bolt should aim to maintain close communication with the Council and, where possible, help shape its decision-making. It will want to discourage the Council from seeing abandonment of the process as the simplest way forward. However, this requires careful handling - Bolt is at the beginning of what it hopes will be a long-term commercial relationship and will want to avoid coming across as too aggressive or forceful.
* Ideally, the Council will apply to the court for an interim order to lift the automatic suspension, allowing it to proceed with signing the contract with Bolt. Bolt should consider using any commercial influence it has to encourage the Council to take this step.
* Bolt should be mindful that if the Council is able to extend its current contract with the incumbent provider, it may be in no hurry to take a decision on abandonment *or* apply to lift the automatic suspension. It may watch and wait for the claimant to approach it with a request for settlement. In that scenario, Bolt should continue to engage with the Council on pre-Contract matters, both in order to prepare for the commencement of the Contract and to ensure it is positioning itself as a key partner.

{color:#0747a6}+*LEGAL PROCESS*+{color}

* Procurement cases are specifically addressed in the Technology and Construction Court Guide (the “Guide”), alongside the Civil Procedure Rules (CPR). This case will be heard in the Technology and Construction Court (TCC). 
* The next step is for Lime to serve its Particulars of Claim, which will provide more detail about the basis of its case. Lime may divide its pleadings into confidential and non-confidential sections. The court and the Council will see both, but Bolt may only be given access to the non-confidential version. This approach is intended to protect commercially sensitive information - particularly important if the procurement process is later restarted.
* A defendant must file an Acknowledgment of Service within 14 days of receiving the claim form. The defence must then be filed within either 14 days of receiving the Particulars of Claim, or 28 days if an Acknowledgment of Service has been submitted. In Bolt’s case, as it has been served as an interested party, it should now consider whether it wants to take part in the proceedings. If so, it should notify the court accordingly.
* A Case Management Conference (CMC) will be scheduled to set the timetable for the case and to deal with any applications—such as a request to lift the automatic suspension.
* Typically, the first CMC is arranged within 14 days of the Acknowledgement of Service or the Defence being filed. It is usually set far enough in advance to give the parties time to complete their disclosure and cost budgeting obligations.
* If any party needs to delay the CMC, they can write to the judge’s clerk with an explanation of why a later date would be appropriate.
* In procurement cases, it is common for there to be early applications for disclosure (i.e. the sharing of key documents relevant to the case), and this is sometimes dealt with before an application to lift the automatic suspension. The Guide encourages contracting authorities to provide important decision-making material at a very early stage in the proceedings. As a result, the Council may proactively share relevant documents relating to Bolt’s tender with Lime. Bolt could engage with the Council and ask to see copies of, or be updated on, any disclosure.

{color:#0747a6}+*TUPE*+{color}

*While the standstill period is over (it came to an end on commencement of these proceedings), we are now in the period of automatic suspension, during which the Contract cannot be entered into (until the court decides otherwise).*

* There is no fixed timeline for how long the automatic suspension will remain in place. It largely depends on whether the Council decides to apply to the court for an interim order (a temporary ruling) to lift the suspension. Please refer to the  earlier comments on the importance of Bolt engaging with the Council to help influence its decision on this point.
* You’ve asked how this affects the timeline and obligations under the Transfer of Undertakings (Protection of Employment) Regulations 2006 (“TUPE”). Under TUPE, employees would transfer from the current provider to Bolt on the date the services themselves transfer. This means that any delay in the handover of services will also delay the TUPE transfer. Employees will only move to Bolt once the services officially transfer. Assuming the Council continues using the current provider during the automatic suspension period, that provider would be expected to keep the affected employees in place until the transfer occurs.

*In terms of TUPE-related obligations that apply before the transfer date, the regulations set out several duties:*

# *The current provider* (the incumbent) must give information to, and where necessary consult with, the affected employees or their representatives ahead of the transfer.
# The current provider must also give Bolt certain employee-related details - known as *Employee Liability Information* - at least 28 days before the transfer. This includes key information about the employees who will transfer.
# *Bolt*, as the incoming provider, must inform the current provider of any planned changes (referred to in TUPE as *“measures”*) that it expects to make in connection with the transfer.

“Measures” could include proposed changes to terms and conditions of employment, working hours, or other aspects of the employees’ roles.

There are no set deadlines under TUPE for the obligations described in sections 3.4.1 (employee consultation) and 3.4.3 (notification of proposed measures).

{color:#ff5630}*In practice, we would expect any TUPE-related activity to be paused during the automatic suspension period. The current provider may prefer to wait until there is clarity about the transfer date and confirmation that Bolt will be the new provider before continuing discussions with affected employees.*{color}

* We recommend that Bolt stays in close contact with the Council regarding pre-contract matters as needed. That said, the Council and the current provider may ultimately decide to pause the TUPE process until the suspension is resolved.

{color:#0747a6}+*TIMELINE FOR THIS TYPE OF LEGAL CHALLENGE, AND ADVISE ON THE EARLIEST LIKELY RESOLUTION DATE?*+{color}

Either party could seek for the case to be appointed to the shorter and flexible trial procedure. Under this procedure, a Case Management Conference must take place within 12 weeks of Acknowledgement of Service and the trial within eight months of the CMC.

However, under the normal procedure, current court availability suggests that a first CMC would not take place before October 2025. It is then likely to be over 12 months until the trial, and it could be beyond this. However, the parties could apply to the court to expedite the process. 

After a trial, a judgment can be between 3 to 12 months, although the TCC seeks to issue its decisions promptly.

However, from Bolt’s perspective, the key dates will be the automatic suspension being lifted, and the Contract being entered into. Once that has been done, the Contract will be effective, and the litigation may be of less significance (although Bolt may still wish to remain up to date on the litigation). If the automatic suspension is not lifted, then the trial is much more likely to be expedited.

{color:#0747a6}+*INTERESTED PARTY*+{color}

* Lime has served the claim form on Bolt because it is considered an interested party. The Court Guide recognises that a winning bidder, like Bolt, may have a legitimate interest in the outcome of procurement challenges.
* An interested party can apply to become a full party to the case, meaning it would take an active role in the proceedings. However, the Guide also makes clear that the court can usually take an interested party’s position into account without them formally joining the case.
* The Guide requires the main parties to keep interested parties informed about anything that could affect them. Either the Council or Lime could apply to formally add Bolt to the proceedings, or Bolt could choose to make that application itself.
* If an interested party wishes to be formally represented in the case, it should apply as soon as reasonably possible. This is typically done by sending a written application - often in the form of a letter to the court and providing copies to all other parties involved.
* The application should explain the level of involvement being requested, such as asking for access to legal documents (pleadings) or the ability to file submissions. It’s also helpful to inform the other parties in advance if you intend to participate, and this can be noted in the application itself.
* The court may decide whether an interested party is allowed to take part in specific applications, hearings, or issues, and it may also place limits on how the party can be involved. It is ultimately up to the court to determine the extent of that involvement.
* An interested party, like Bolt, may be entitled to recover legal costs or, in some cases, may be required to pay them.
* Regardless of the court’s decision, Bolt can still engage directly with the Council to support its defence in the case.
* Bolt may be able to support the Council in defending its position through engagement with the Council. This will depend on the relationship with the Council, and its position in the litigation.
* Bolt can either seek to become a defendant to the action, or become an interested party, and from either position seek to put forward its position. One consideration as to whether Bolt should participate is that a specific limb of Lime’s claim, as set out at paragraph 5.1 of the claim form) is focussed on Bolt’s pricing. How this is positioned in the particulars of claim may influence how involved Bolt wishes to become.

*Country-specific restrictions or legal considerations:*
Once the liquidation is formally approved by shareholders, notarized, and registered with the Public Registry of Commerce, the company may no longer engage in any new transactions or business activities.

*Timeline:*
There is no fixed timeline. The duration depends on the complexity (assets, liabilities, contracts, etc.). If there are no significant obligations, liquidation may proceed quickly. Key timing elements:

* Notarization and registration of initial resolutions: usually takes 2–3 weeks, depending on the notary.
* Publication of the final liquidation balance sheet: 15 days for creditor/shareholder review.
* Approval and notarization of final resolutions: another 2–3 weeks.
* Deregistration with tax and labor authorities: depends on official processing times, which can be delayed.
During this phase, tax returns (even if zero) must continue to be filed, and the company must remain in full compliance to avoid delays.

*Liquidator:*
A Mexican tax resident with valid Tax ID and accounting expertise must be appointed as a liquidator of the company. Typically, this is an individual accountant or accounting firm. Upon appointment, the liquidator becomes the sole legal representative, responsible for:

* Preparing the inventory of assets/liabilities;
* Concluding contracts and liquidating assets;
* Drafting the final liquidation balance sheet and distributing any equity;
* Cancelling tax and labor registrations;
* Keeping records for 10 years for potential audits.

One principal matter remaining however is liability, namely:

* 6.2 provides for a general mutual liability cap (12 months GMV) they want to turn one-sided. We’re basically fine playing around with it a bit, e.g. saying that “12 months gmv or 50k whichever is higher”, but we wouldn’t and shouldn’t allow this to be uncapped and it should apply mutually - the financial risk from the unknown needs to be limited for both parties. Even if the scope is limited to direct damages only and the likelihood of materialization is deemed remote.
* That goes hand in hand with their request for 6.4 where they have elaborated on the types of risks Bolt should cater for. While we could principally discuss providing e.g. double the cap for confidentiality and privacy breaches which result in direct damages to Temenos (6.4.2) then the overall cap (6.4.1) and the IP infringement (6.4.3 - totally irrelevant btw) should be limited by a general cap. And in each case apply mutually.

*Message to Temenos could be:*

*_We are unable to accept the changes to 6.2 and 6.4 - please see in the draft attached. We’re happy to discuss and address any practical concerns related to specific risks but as for the general risk from the unknown (which the suggested amendments seem to be addressing) then the financial risk needs to be limited for both parties equally._*

Cheers

If we compare Oslo D1.08 V122 focus group against the rest of the Oslo D1.08 fleet (excl. focus group), we indeed do not see much of a difference in errors causing collections. 

* We *keep seeing E2* in low quantities - it has neither increased nor decreased following the update.
* We *keep seeing motor-specific errors* (E258 phase error, E261 hall error, E264 ecu mosfet error, E274 hall supply error). Again, the errors were not consistent before, and they do not appear to having reduced following the update.

*Errors for D1.08 V122 Oslo focus group (14.04-01.05):*

!image-20250502-145421.png|width=1188,height=718,alt="image-20250502-145421.png"!

*Errors for D1.08 excl. V122 Oslo focus group (14.04-01.05):*

!image-20250502-145125.png|width=1190,height=720,alt="image-20250502-145125.png"!

An overview of error distribution of different categories shows us that ~60% of the time we act on items related to critical system errors (E1/E2), Motor and ECU errors and battery errors (E3, E530 id pin lost). A remarkable amount of errors are triggered by the lighting system - 26%. Throttle and brake lever errors are also critical, but accumulate to only <4% of collections. Helmet & hatch lock errors accumulate ~7% of collections.

It makes sense to discuss together with the powertrain team and evaluate which categories we could deprioritize to reduce collections for errors which technically have little impact on user experience, availability & GMV.

The driver deduction feature is a feature that removes from a driver's balance funds that were wrongly/intentionally charged by drivers on riders during a trip. It is a feature on Beehive that recoups funds drivers wrongly/intentionally charged on trips.

*Intention*

The driver deductions feature is intended to, amongst other things: 

* reduce our costs by retrieving monies wrongly charged on riders(monies will be retrieved from driver balances to replace refunds issued to customers) and 
* help to measure/monitor improvement in drivers’ behaviours by taking appropriate measures(including retraining, temporary and/or permanent blocks, etc.) on recalcitrant drivers.

Over a long period, “_I was charged more than expected”_ complaints from riders have severely impacted not only our metrics(CSAT, case count, etc.) but also the amount of compensation we dole out. The majority of these complaints from riders turn out to be true after investigations as drivers either disregard discounts or cause overcharges through fraudulent means like manipulating the app or its features, use of longer routes, etc.

When this happens, we compensate the riders and additionally get a bad rating on the ticket, negatively impacting our CSAT while losing money through no means caused by us. The drivers? They go free. The amounts compensated riders WoW, MoM is our cost, we don't get it back. On the back of this are _Rider did not pay_ reports from drivers.

*Statistics:*

CSAT(Target - 85%) -

Jan: 81.32% | Feb: 82.11% | March: 79.94%

COMPENSATION AMOUNT -

Jan: 66 cases - GHS 3,487 | Feb: 70 cases - GHS 3,754| March: 184 cases - GHS 10,911.2

These amounts were compensations for drivers reporting false rider did not pay when investigations and evidence received confirmed payment were made by the riders.

The feature is available on driver tickets, where we can deduct wrongly charged amounts and even select the party at fault (Driver or Bolt); however, it is not available on rider tickets. This unavailability means that to deduct wrongly charged amounts from drivers' balances, an agent would have to create an outgoing ticket, which is an additional cost. Meanwhile, outgoing tickets have been discontinued across all markets in @Laimdota Vilistere’s region due to cost concerns. 

So essentially, we are compensating riders for _I was charged more than expected_ caused by drivers and false _rider did not pay reports_ from drivers and losing money simultaneously, which in turn impacts our GMV negatively. However, if drivers know they will be deducted and/or sanctioned for wrongful charges, they will be measured in any unapproved/unwarranted charge of a rider and will not spread it to other drivers. 

The driver's experience will not be impacted as such drivers will be aware and desist from it and especially not spread it to other drivers. Furthermore, not every driver is going to be targeted as not all of them are engaged in such activities, it is strictly those who engage in it. Lastly, it is going to work the same as other provisions in our terms and conditions hence will not have any impact on them.

*Urgency and Timeline*

The deadline to access this feature as soon as possible. When implemented, the feature will help:

* Reduce and balance costs as monies given out through refunds will be recouped, placing our GMV in good standing.
* Measure, monitor (the impact of) activities of drivers and apply the appropriate measures on erring drivers, serve as a reminder to others to adhere to our terms and desist from irregular activities.
* Save and improve our metrics (CSAT, case count as compared to forecasted figures, TRT, etc.).
* Reduce/stop rider churn and loss of market share through constant overcharges by drivers.

A lot of effort invested into exploration of this topic and testing various approaches (polynomial fitting, isotonic regression, cubic splines, …). To reiterate: the main goal here is to fit a smooth curve to the pymc outputs (e.g. gmv ip, gmv pip, gmv next month) as these are inherently non smooth due to the nature of the bayesian approach. This is problematic for the optimization, as it requires monotonic data. While the algorithms we tested do result in smooth variants of e.g. GMV IP, the calculated uplifts (e.g. GMV uplift which is delta(GMV IP + GMV PIP) between investment and baseline scenario) are not necessarily smooth.

Market manager is not the best fit for Rentals, as they are very immature domain as for now.

*Overview*

There are several city groups (some with a single city) that have targeting campaigns. Each group has different properties, such as maximum cap, discount, and code usage limits. Currently, these campaigns are structured on a monthly basis, with the goal of transitioning to a weekly schedule. Every month, a single analyst reviews the previous month’s results and manually adjusts the properties for each city group one by one. There is no automated method for determining how to adjust the parameters for the upcoming spend period; these decisions are based solely on the analyst's insights and experience. Additionally, the list of cities within each group often changes, with some cities being added or removed.

To streamline the process, all these campaigns are currently organised within a single large Bulk Group, which is copied each month as a simplest solution possible.

*Pain points after migrating to Market Manager (the Rides way):*

# *Increased workload:* 
There are multiple city groups to manage, rather than having everything in one place (one BG).
# *Frequent adjustments:* 
When campaigns are copied month over month, changes are very frequent, leaving little room for automation.
# *Insufficient input data:* 
There is a lack of input data to automate decision-making effectively.

*Other considered options:*

# *Enable actions inside the bulk group editor and use the previous month’s BG as ‘template’.*
This will not resolve issues, as there is no common action across all markets and currencies. In some markets, the list of cities still needs to be adjusted manually.
# *Build a spreadsheet importer*
Define a BG inside a spreadsheet with limited parameters changing over the next periods. 
This is not ideal, as it would be a temporary solution and require several weeks of engineering time to implement.
# *Simplify BG editing week over week.*
This could be achieved with a custom action that would work as a simplified view on top of BG editing. The user would only see:
{{[array of cities] : params {max cap: XX, discount: YY%, no. usages: ZZ}}}
This approach seems the best way to reduce overhead for Rentals. However, it’s definitely not the initial idea of onboarding them on Market Manager. It’s rather like building a dedicated, simplified UI on top of Market Manager features.

Hi [~accountid:5b7be9e6b8e3cb589585eb47] , Thanks for the input throughout this ticket. After reviewing the available facts and responses, I’m closing this case with the following conclusions and next steps.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Incident summary*
{panel}

This was a dual issue:

# Disclosure of a third-party phone number (person B) to the account holder (person A)
# Suspicious activity on the user’s account, potentially indicating unauthorized access or a recycled number issue

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Conclusion*
{panel}

# *Data disclosure (phone number shared)*
The agent shared the phone number of another user (person B) with the affected user (person A) to help identify unusual login activity. While the intent was to assist, this constitutes a privacy violation. Phone numbers should not be disclosed to any third party under any circumstances.

* The phone number was shared via chat and cannot be removed from the message history.
* The agent was advised to ask the user not to retain or use the phone number.

This is a minor data disclosure involving a single data point, caused by human error. It is contained and does not require regulatory reporting.

# *Suspicious account activity*

* The account had new devices added.
* One ride was taken.
* No changes were made to personal data.
* The correct phone number remains associated with the account.
* All sessions have since been logged out.
While the root cause is not definitively confirmed, this could relate to recycled number scenarios. However, the impact is low and there is no evidence of malicious access.

This does not qualify as a reportable data breach under GDPR.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Actions taken*
{panel}

* Sessions were logged out
* Phone number was not changed
* The user was advised to disregard and delete the disclosed number
* Incident will be documented in the internal tracker

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Final notes* 
{panel}

Please remind CS agents that personal data, including phone numbers, must not be shared with other users, even when attempting to resolve login or device issues.

This case will now be closed.

Hey [~accountid:641d5e830e6828ab20269e6d] 

The Whatsapp integration is already up for over a year. My question wasn't about integrating Whatsapp as an OTP sender, the question was about the consent structure.
Uber and other platforms basically say something like "By proceeding, you consent to receive a One Time Password through one of the following channels: <SMS/RCS, Whatsapp, calls, Viber....>, and then they chose which channel is the most appropriate to the user, through a fallback scenario.

While at Bolt the user needs a specific consent on each method. Select SMS, to consent to SMS and we will send an SMS, or select Whatsapp to consent to Whatsapp and we will send a Whatsapp. It doesn't allow for our systems to chose the most appropriate channel to authenticate a phone number automatically.



I’ll go through your questions below:

Before we advise, can you please help us understand some parts:

* am I correct that we will use this channel ONLY for sending the OTP code, eg we do not anticipate any integration with the marketing team systems where they would send marketing to whatsapp based on your project?
** *We are sending Whatsapp only for OTP codes. I am not aware if LCM uses it for any other scenario, however if that happens, it is not through the Product-Platform Whatsapp channel which is exclusive to OTPs*



* How does the flow of verifying that a user has these apps look like? Are we correct that we do not access the device?
** If not, will there be any type of integration with Whatsapp? Which one?
** *Currently we use 2 methods:*
*** *1- Whatsapp by choice: On Phone Authentication, the user is displayed a radio choice between SMS and Whatsapp. If Whatsapp is chosen, we will send an OTP code through Whatsapp. The code is sent through a registered OTP sender with META (only OTPs can be sent through there, and we are identified as a Meta Verified Profile)*
*** *2- Whatsapp as priority: On over 100 countries on Android alone, we check if Whatsapp is installed in the device, through a META supported code. No options are given. If Whatsapp is detected we will send the code through Whatsapp. If this sendout fails we fallback to SMS (this fallback currently requires improvement). When the OTP code is received, it will be automatically input in the app, either it’s received by SMS or Whatsapp.*
** Did we consider cases when a user, in theory, has these apps linked to their phone number, but does not have it installed on the device?
*** *Yes, in these cases the Whatsapp OTP will time-out and an SMS will be sent as a fallback*
** Example, when I use Yandex Go in Belarus, they send their OTP to Viber, but I do not have it installed and do not use it. It’s a major issue when you are in rush and need a taxi.
*** *They should fallback to SMS as we do* 🙂 
** Can we always propose an option to use SMS? It may be proposed once we sent it to Whatsapp and if the user waits for 60 sec and did not receive anything, the user may click on ‘Receive SMS’?
*** *On Option 1, they can chose SMS voluntarily*
*** *On both options, after 30seconds, the user can request a “Resend OTP” SMS is given as a choice, if the previous attempt was Whatsapp*
** It’s also a point to the privacy as Whatsapp/Viber are personal messengers and not all users prefer to obtain any OTP via this.
*** *That is indeed a case. However the reasoning for using Whatsapp is due to privacy and security first and later also lower costs. SMS is not a secured connection. There are plenty of cases of Man in The middle attacks, or simple SMS pumping attacks (attackers can monetise SMS to their gains). On these cases there are financial losses, but on Main in the Middle attacks, fraudsters can and will get hold of our users accounts. We have been warned multiple times - and pushed by AKI (* [~accountid:712020:0b1ccfcb-3809-460a-88ab-c96985ba329a] *) to reduce SMS dependence due to it’s security holes. Whatsapp is an end-to-end encrypted communication, which caters to the users privacy. That’s why we are doing our best to make the authentication funnel as frictionless as possible to our good users, but add friction and remove financial gains to fraudsters.*

*Update per May 5, 2025*

* Discussed with Lifecycle team on the long term plan of the comms development in order to decide to marge the canvases on delivery eater level or product level (restaurant & groceries). *Generally reached consensus that it will be done on delivery eater* and canvases between products will be merged and only split based on eater lifecycle stage. However, there are some concerns to address:
** How can the team personalise the content if we do not know which product users interacted with? Some options brought up during discussion:
*** Based on their RFM per product
*** Based on their last purchase
*** Based on automated recommendation
** Conversion goal is set on canvas level, not node level, therefore, merging canvases of restaurant and groceries highlights the need of tracking multiple conversion in the reporting.
* Created [summary of comms coverage|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1ospehnV0EOFyU2m8fk2A1rdiEgUOdTAE3PMLg9Ex5ow/edit?gid=0#gid=0] of the current lifecycle stage definition vs Growth. In general our auto-comms only reach 25% of users and we are missing out some opportunity such as users who are still active with more than 6 lifetime orders (currently not targeted at all).

+*Next step*+

* LCM will discuss internally on 2 different scenarios of the flow when merged: realistic & ideal. Realistic will be the first iteration with limited customization and ideal will be what the team will improve toward (long term goal).
* LCM will discuss internally the technical implication when merging canvases and how they can set them up in targeting platform.
* A follow-up discussion to understand the segment coverage in our current setup — eg: users who signed up more than X days ago will no longer be targeted, hence lower comms coverage.

Hi Taya, thanks for reaching out!

We discussed this topic with the team and decided that we should *always select the “Let the user decide” option*, even if the user has already mentioned where they want their refund.

* Even if we refund a preferred destination, the user still needs to click a button to accept it, so we don’t speed up the process this way. 
* Letting the user decide the destination prevents us from making any mistakes and avoids misunderstandings if the user tells us their preferred destination but changes their mind.
* This way, we let the user always confirm where they want their refund.

The article already says at the very beginning that “When issuing a refund for a ride that was paid in-app, always choose the _Let User Decide_ option in the Beehive refunds toolkit.”, so we won’t make any updates right now.

Have a great day!

# There are 2 spend types: market place (MP) and user lifecycle (UL).
# Each spend type is split into investment period (IP) and post-investment period (PIP), which makes it 4 different spend types (MP IP, MP PIP, UL IP, UL PIP). This distinction is important for ROI calculation.
# Current approach is:
## Generate set of scenarios with MP spend set to 0%
## Find UL spend using the dataset above (the exact approach is unknown, need to sync with Ninda)
## Generate new set with UL set to the spend above
## Find MP spend using optimization
# The current approach is complicated because of this 2-step selection, and is technically equivalent to just running optimization with constraints over whole dataset.
# Therefore the proposal is to generate 3 sets of (MP spend, UL spend) scenarios and run optimization over this dataset. Each set is a matrix with (MP spend, UL spend) axis, and every point is forecast on the corresponding (MP, UL) spend.
# 3 sets are required to calculate ROI, and therefore driven by ROI formula rules:
## (MP PIP = MP IP, UL PIP = UL IP)
## (MP PIP = MP IP -0.3pp, UL PIP = UL IP)
## (MP PIP = MP IP, UL PIP = UL IP -0.3pp)
# In order to calculate MP ROI we take points from dataset A and B. Similarly, in order to calculate UL ROI we take points from datasets A and C
# Before passing to optimization, scenarios are filtered by spend and ROI constraints.

*FITMENT*

*Spiders*

Both spiders are identical dimensions wise. No fitment issues with either.

*Crank arms*

Also no fitment issues. Wheeltop crank arms produce a slightly narrower Q-factor, but the difference is minor (3mm per side). I did not notice any difference when riding.

____________________________________________________________________________________________________
*CHAINRING SELECTION - ALUMINUM VS STEEL RING*


Aluminum big rings are very-very common on bicycles, so wear rate is probably not an issue really. Road bikes big chainring is similar size than ours (50-52T vs our 48T) and those last easily 25 000km, usually way more. The material is probably higher quality alloy so it is not directly comparable, also wheel size is different. But 25k km is still way more kilometers than our bike will ever do. Plus we have a rear hub motor, so the load on the chain and chainrings will be minimal anyway. (/) 
*According to the supplier*, the steel ring is theoretically more wear-resistant, but they also pointed out that aluminum ring will not rust like a steel chainring does, as the ED coating will wear off on the contact surfaces of the teeth and eventually rust will form. And that they both  _“can pass the 1800N, 100,000 times fatigue endurance test.”_ (/) 
As price is the same and fitment is OK, I would suggest we go with the lightest option, which is aluminum chainring (/)

Hi [~accountid:610a3ee66051c5006aeeeea1] and thanks for the background. Its great that we already have some ground work done which may help us to move faster here. At the outset, we have not had this issue in any of the other markets where Bolt Plus has been rolled out. 

My two cents on the issues highlighted:

# *Express Consent for Early Start of Services (Withdrawal Period)*

To satisfy the requirement for express consent without adding a checkbox or changing the T&Cs, we propose including prominent, plain-language text on the screen immediately before the user clicks “Join now”. The text would state that by clicking “Join now,” the user explicitly agrees to the recurring membership fee, which renews automatically unless cancelled which can be done via the Bolt Plus section of the app. This message is displayed clearly and separately from the bulk of the T&Cs, together with the user’s affirmative action (clicking “Join now”), should be consent enough. From a global perspective I would say this approach has so far proven to be complaint and low-risk. 

h3. *2. 24-Hour Cancellation Limitation During Withdrawal Period*

Although clause 3.1 of the T&Cs imposes a 24-hour cutoff before the renewal date for standard cancellations, this provision does not legally restrict the 14-day right of withdrawal. In practice, any user who exercises their withdrawal right within 14 days (via the model form or Bolt App cancellation flow) would still receive a prorated or full refund, depending on whether services were used. Since Section 3.2 already provides for a refund during the withdrawal period, and Bolt honors this in customer support handling, no T&C update is needed. 

h3. *3. Undefined “Significant Changes”*

While the T&Cs state that customers will be notified of “significant changes,” they do not define what counts as “significant.” To avoid ambiguity, we interpret this term broadly in practice and notify users of *any change* that affects price, service scope, or benefits. This operational practice of broad interpretation mitigates the risk of consumer challenge or regulatory scrutiny, even without a change to the T&Cs. This approach is common in app-based service models where contract updates are pushed via email and in-app notices. For Malta, this soft compliance posture is proportionate to the legal exposure.

h3. *4. Responsible Trader Identity*

The T&Cs correctly identify *Bolt Operations OÜ* as the responsible trader, and this is consistent throughout the document. There is no issue to address here, and this meets all formal requirements under Maltese consumer protection law.

Hello Team!

I completely understand why this might look like a double charge, but I can assure you that the user was only charged once. This is a common part of how card payments are processed. Here's what happens:

# When the user first makes a payment, the bank temporarily ‘reserves' the funds and this is just the bank setting aside the amount for the transaction. The user’s account balance might show less amount but the payment hasn’t actually been taken out by the bank yet.
# Later, when the payment is fully processed, that reserved amount is now “officially” debited from the user’s account. At that point, some banks send a second notification, which can make it seem like a second charge.


I would advise the user to check their final account balance or statement, where they can confirm that only one payment was actually withdrawn. The earlier “pending” amount will either drop off or convert into the final charge.

Cheers,
Afiba

Hi [~accountid:61268a403ef46a00706be25d] , thank you for the clarification and follow-up. Based on the facts provided, we can now formally close this case with the following conclusions:

*_Incident summary_*

An outsourcing agent mistakenly disclosed the full name of a Bolt internal employee (Vasile-Ciprian Oita) to an external fleet representative. The agent was meant to provide the name of a driver within the fleet but instead referenced the employee responsible for blocking the driver. The disclosure was made via Beehive and could not be deleted, as Beehive does not support message deletion from the recipient's side once sent via email.

*_Assessment and classification_*

* One internal employee's name was shared externally.
* This qualifies as a minor personal data disclosure due to human error.
* The disclosure was accidental, limited in scope, and contained.
* No sensitive data or contact information was shared.
* The issue was flagged, and feedback was provided.

This does not meet the threshold for reporting to the data protection authority.

*_Next steps_*

* No further action is required beyond internal documentation.
* The incident will be logged internally.
* Please remind relevant agents and outsourcing partners to avoid referencing internal staff names in external communications unless explicitly required and approved.

[~accountid:5f3fd4a53e9e2e004d00d008], [~accountid:5b1e0603d8714649c69c5abf], [~accountid:6012c28a3b1af00069a0c0a7]  and [~accountid:5e7dbc6c89b73b0c330596c0]  recently discussed Builder service dashboards. The problem is that Builder does not show some valuable K8S metadata and logs, so possible problems are not visible to the users.

An alternative is to deploy a ready-made K8S dashboard service and grant Builder users access to it. Although it can cover all the needs nicely out of the box, it has some drawbacks, such as:

* a risk of K8S control plane overload due to separate queries from every dashboard,
* complex and unclear access control.

The Builder's advantage is that it collects all the required metadata once and can then show it to any user when needed without additional K8S requests. We agreed to keep this concept.

How does this affect this ticket?

* We don’t reject it due to an intended migration to a separate dashboard,
* We keep the cluster metadata “cache” ({{cluster_status}}) in Builder,
* We will likely extend the {{cluster_status}} with more fields/metadata.

At the same time, we did not find a strong reason to move the {{cluster_status}}storage to Redis or something else.

So we agreed that the most optimal solution would be to create a Data Archiver job to automatically clean up the outdated records. This would also help to avoid handling very old records of a legacy data structure (i.e. missing some fields).

Hi [~accountid:61d5747249f19500694358eb] 

Croatian Civil Obligations Act provides that the owner of a dangerous item or activity may be held strictly liable (without fault) for damage caused by that item.

However, the owner can be exempt from liability if they can prove the damage was caused:

* By force majeure,
* Solely by the actions of the injured party, or
* Solely by a *third party whose actions could not have been foreseen or prevented -* but the owner needs to be able to prove this.

There is currently no case law or explicit legal definition in Croatia that confirms whether e-scooters qualify as “opasna stvar” (dangerous items) under Civil act. Courts may assess this on a case-by-case basis.

I have prepared an answer to the counterparty’s lawyer but please note that this might not prevent them from initiating court proceedings against Bolt. In case they do initiate a court proceedings, our chances of success are below 40% and we will still need to pay their legal fees.

+*🔹 Format 1 – LMDCVTC-led Freelance Ops*+

# Can you confirm that LMDCVTC freelancers _never_ access Bolt’s internal systems or data?
# Does Bolt influence processing parameters (e.g., who is contacted, what is said, timing)? 

*Advice:*

* If LMDCVTC uses its own data independently and Bolt only receives aggregated or anonymised outputs, no DPA or NDA is needed. Otherwise, if we will review driver-level information (personal data), we will need to conclude a data sharing agreement.

+*🔹 Format 2 – Student Platforms (StaffMe / Campus Consulting)*+

*Privacy Assessment:*

# Is there a data processing agreement/T&C between Bolt and the student platforms? I’d need to review those clauses.
# Are freelancers individually onboarded and bound by sufficient contractual and confidentiality terms?
# How is access to Bolt’s database granted and logged? Is it time-limited and purpose-bound? What systems are accesses given to? What data do they receive.

*Advice:*

* An NDA alone is insufficient. If freelancers process personal data on Bolt’s behalf, a DPA (data processing agreement) or equivalent obligations must be embedded in the agreement with the platform.
* Ensure access rights are based on need-to-know, and revoke access immediately after the task.

+*🔹 Format 3 – Direct Freelance Hires*+

*Privacy Assessment:*

* Freelancers are likely processors acting under our instruction

# Are freelancers trained on data protection? Are they required to follow Bolt’s internal privacy policies?
# What technical and organizational measures are in place to supervise and limit data access? What systems and what data do they have access to?

*Advice:*

* If freelancers are processing personal data under Bolt’s instructions, they are processors. A DPA and NDA are required, plus internal onboarding that includes privacy and security protocols.

When we create a new Supplier in Workday, we are able to put restrictions on the supplier in term of company or company hierarchy.

- If there are no restrictions applied, all companies will be able to see the supplier.

- In P2P, we can restrict all South African suppliers with their own company, this will ensure that when we raise Purchase Requests in other entities, they will not be able to see South African suppliers.

This is for both Requisitions, Purchase Order and Supplier Invoices.

Below is the table of reaction time based on the data extracted from Vianova, which is the same dashboard used by the City of Basel.



*  For the 1st warning in January, the average was 17.6 hours. 
* For the 2nd warning in March, Vianova’s data shows an average reaction time of 7.4 hours.

*These numbers differ significantly from the city's reported times, especially in March where there is a 26h discrepancy.*

Regarding the event specific restricted zones, which were said to be overcrowded and not implemented on time, the city has not provided any supporting evidence, unlike the Markthalle NPZ case, referenced in the email shared by Jeno, where documentation was made available. 
In our case, the zones were fully integrated into our system and cleared before the start of the event. One limitation to note is that we did not send confirmation emails documenting the implementation of the zones at that time. This practice was only introduced after the second warning. However, it is also important to mention that we never received any feedback or indication from the city stating that the zones had not been implemented correctly during or after the event. We have complete data in Looker confirming the clearance of the zones (below, a visual representation of the tasks completed in Kepler) .
However, I am not certain whether this internal data is acceptable as formal evidence.

The Vianova platform contains anyway the full logs of all infringements, including those related to event zones and the corresponding reaction times. Based on this data, we believe we can demonstrate that our vehicles did not disrupt the designated event areas as claimed by the city.

*A) Bolt-Owned Fleet (Mirrors setup like Bolt Services France SARL)*

h4. 1. *Wholly Owned Subsidiary*

* *Company A is created by Bolt*
* Bolt is the *sole shareholder*
* *Director of A is a Bolt employee*
* *OR* director of A is *not* a Bolt employee 

----

h3. *B) Employee-Owned Fleet*

h4. 2. *Bolt Employee as Owner*

* *Company B is created by a Bolt employee*, using personal assets
* Bolt is *not* a shareholder
* *Director of B is the same Bolt employee*
* *OR* director is someone else

----

h3. *C) Hybrid or Other Ownership Models*

h4. 3. *Bolt Minority Stake*

* Bolt owns a *minority stake* in a fleet-owning company
* *Fleet is managed independently*
* *Directors are not Bolt employees*

h4. 4. *Independent Owner*

* Fleet owned by an *individual with no personal or employment link* to Bolt

h4. 5. *Related Individual Owner*

* Fleet owned by a *past employee* or *relative of a current/past Bolt employee*

h4. 6. *Employee Collective Ownership*

* Fleet owned by *multiple current Bolt employees*

*Another consideration applicable to all models:*

* Bolt employees (e.g., like @begona.serrano in Spain) *may advise or support* these fleet operators, without direct control.

{quote}As my internal team continues to analyze the system activity, some interesting patterns are emerging.
Please consider the following.

# Metrics collection:

This activity shows spikes that align very neatly with the spikes we are seeing. It runs on the whole every 20-30 seconds
but seems to have some larger aggregation or similar activity every 14 minutes, with activity counts similar to the following:

20:00: 13,330 operations
20:14: 12,963 operations
20:28: 13,111 operations

# Service account token creation

There is a large volume of these calls as well. The pattern is less aligned with the spikes in general, though it does occur
during the spikes and would certainly contribute to the CPU usage. My team did not provide specific activity counts for
this, however.

# Garbage collection

While this is an expected activity, it, like the service account token activity, it runs at regular intervals and costs a non-negligible
amount of CPU.

The best explanation for the spikes at this time, when all of this is taken together, is that the accumulated CPU cost of all of the above,
in line with the high metrics collection activity spike on the same cadence as the CPU spikes, are creating the scenario.

I have asked my team what they have in the way of recommendation for remediation, I will let you know when I hear back
from them on that. In the meantime, please do not hesitate to reach out again.{quote}

*General consideration:* from a tax compliance and risk management perspective, branding bonuses should only be paid to companies that:

* Are registered on the platform as service providers,
* Hold all necessary licenses to operate transport services, and
* Are actually providing services and operating vehicles that generate the bonus.

*Why payments should go only to the actual operating service provider:*

# *Substantiation of business purpose:*
Branding bonuses are incentives for companies actively participating in and promoting the platform. If the payment is made to a party that does not provide any services or engage with the platform, *the economic rationale of the payment is questionable* and may be reclassified by tax authorities as non-deductible or non-genuine. This leads us to points 2 and 3.
# *Risk of undeclared income:*
If subcontractors earn the actual operational income, this structure can facilitate undeclared income and tax leakage. *The platform may be seen as facilitating tax evasion through a shell entity* (e.g. SIA Auto).
# *Lack of transparency & tax deductibility:*
Paying entities that are not registered on the platform obstructs auditability. That is, the platform may *not be able to demonstrate a clear performance-to-payment link*, which is essential for defending the legitimacy of such business expenses.
This should be checked with the tax team, but typically, payments made to facilitate business (such as bonuses or commissions) are deductible for corporate income tax purposes if they are:

* Incurred exclusively for business purposes;
* Properly documented (e.g. invoices, contracts); and
* Paid to a legitimate recipient, and the payment has *economic substance*.

To determine economic substance, authorities look past the legal form of an agreement to its actual purpose and effect. If we sign a branding bonus agreement with a company that is not registered on the platform, does not operate vehicles, and has sublicensed its operations (i.e. is effectively a shell company), then - from a tax authority’s point of view - *the agreement may lack economic substance.*
As a result, *the bonus may not be deductible or could be recharacterized as a non-business expense* or seen as an attempt to shift income for tax evasion purposes.

That being said, *Scheme II* looks riskier to me from a compliance perspective than *Scheme I*. Paying bonuses to a shell company (e.g. SIA Auto) that has no actual operations should not be permitted.

* Will the leased vehicles appear under SIA AUTO or SIA Taxi 1/2 in our platform records?
* What kind of service will SIA AUTO provide to SIA Taxi 1/2 under the _Apkalpošanas līgums_?

Due to complexity of setup we did not create an A/B test for these markets, instead we reverted their activation setups to country level from 1st May and we will observe the change in 

# YoY new user conversion
# # of users that signup in one city but activate in another city

Hi [~accountid:60bf496ea01e11006ac62a66] , and thanks for everyone’s helpful input.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Following a privacy review and confirmation from the legal team, here's our position:*
{panel}

* Drivers operate as independent data controllers. Bolt does not mandate nor prohibit the installation of CCTV systems. When drivers choose to install such equipment, they are fully responsible for ensuring compliance with applicable data protection laws, including providing notice to data subjects (e.g. visible stickers, privacy notices).
* We cannot advise or dictate which camera types to use or how drivers should install them. However, we may *remind* drivers of their legal obligations and refer them to available guidance (global templates and existing KBs).
* For riders, we recommend continuing to use the template already published in Beehive [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/23948|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/23948]. This explains the independent controller model and sets expectations around privacy.
* While legal review covers data protection, safety concerns about visibility or driver distraction from multiple screens is not a legal/privacy issue per-se, and therefore should sit with Local Ops.

Finally, I do not recommend creating local Malta-specific comms or policies unless legally required. This avoids fragmentation and ensures consistency across markets. If recurrent complaints arise, we can consider a non-binding reminder campaign for drivers and fleet owners reiterating their privacy obligations.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}

*Problem Description:*

During testing, we discovered discrepancies between the information displayed on the {{City Area Statistics}} page in the admin panel and the data used for fleet cap calculations for deployment/rebalance.

*Possible Cause:*

# On the {{City Area Statistics}} admin panel page, the number of scooters is calculated based on the {{statistical_area_id}} field from the {{vehicle_state}} table.
# For fleet cap calculations, we use in-memory data about the number of operational vehicles within a statistical area. This also includes logic to determine how many scooters are located within a deployment spot.

During prelive testing, these two calculations showed slight differences, prompting an investigation into the root cause and how it can be addressed.

*Known Issue with Using* {{statistical_area_id}} *from* {{vehicle_state}}*:*

If a vehicle is located at the intersection of two or more statistical areas, only one {{statistical_area_id}} will be recorded, which can lead to inaccuracies in the statistics.

Hello Team!

I completely understand why this might look like a double charge, but I can assure you that the user was only charged once. This is a common part of how card payments are processed. Here's what happens:

# When the user first makes a payment, the bank temporarily ‘reserves' the funds and this is just the bank setting aside the amount for the transaction. The user’s account balance might show less amount but the payment hasn’t actually been taken out by the bank yet.
# Later, when the payment is fully processed, that reserved amount is now “officially” debited from the user’s account. At that point, some banks send a second notification, which can make it seem like a second charge.


I would advise the user to check their final account balance or statement, where they can confirm that only one payment was actually withdrawn. The earlier “pending” amount will either drop off or convert into the final charge within 14 days after the payment.

Regarding how the payment is displayed by the user’s bank is entirely dependent on the bank and Bolt has no control over it. This payment was processed with the right merchant account for Food delivery.

Cheers,
Afiba

Some thoughts from [~accountid:712020:a7a7d4bc-10ca-44a0-a22e-fa8752330abd] 

* *_Unclear rules around automated decision-making (Article 22) create a lot of grey areas_* 
** It's tough to know whether certain platform features, like automated pricing or fraud detection, count as “solely automated decisions” with a significant effect on users. We often overcompensate to stay safe, which slows down product development and makes it harder to launch features consistently across markets.
** The “legal or similarly significant effect” threshold is unclear and inconsistently applied - We often can’t tell whether a decision like temporary deactivation, pricing adjustments, or lower visibility in search results meets this threshold. Different regulators interpret it differently, which makes it hard to scale compliance across markets.
** *_RoPA is more of a checkbox exercise than something useful_* 
*** Maintaining detailed records of all processing activities takes a lot of effort, especially in fast-moving environments. But the actual business or compliance value of those records is often minimal.
* *_Data minimisation and purpose limitation rules are too rigid for how tech companies work_*
** We collect data to provide services, but it's also useful for improving models or flagging harmful behaviour. The GDPR makes it really hard to reuse that data, even when it's in the user’s interest. The lack of clear rules around what's a "compatible purpose" creates internal blockers and complicates our governance processes.
* *_Joint controllership rules don’t reflect how modern partnerships work_*
** Whenever we work with third parties, there's confusion over who’s a controller and what needs to go into the contract. That leads to long negotiations and conservative agreements that don’t match the actual risk or reality.
* *_Strict purpose limitation makes it hard to iterate on products_* 
** When we want to adapt a feature based on how users are interacting with it, it can trigger a full re-assessment of the original processing purpose. This slows down teams and creates friction in product development.
* *_Cross-border data transfers are still a huge blocker_*
** Even with new SCCs, we still have to do transfer impact assessments for most vendors. The rules are unclear and unevenly enforced, and this adds a lot of overhead without improving privacy outcomes. A more practical, risk-based approach would go a long way.
